name: Grid peak calls, sealed the day before and scored the day after
buyer: Factories and data centres whose grid bill is set by their load during a few peak hours
who: Factories and data centres whose grid bill is set by their load during a few peak hours.
note: BORN NOT FOR SALE 2026-08-25 (dated from the newest rows in the recorder's own store, not from this machine's clock, which reads two different days depending which setting is asked). WHAT THE LANE DOES: a factory or data centre's grid bill for a whole year is largely set by how much it was pulling during a handful of hours -- the hours when the whole grid was at its busiest. Once a day, for the day after, the recorder reads the grid operator's own published forecast and writes down one of two things: cut your load, or ordinary day. That is a call. It is sealed with a fingerprint at the moment it is made, before anyone knows how the day went, and it is scored afterwards against the operator's own record of what actually happened -- wrong calls included, one row per call. NOTHING HAS EVER BEEN SOLD HERE and there is no price on the page. The lane's own spec describes a possible paid product later (the calls themselves, ahead of the day) but that is a separate decision that has not been made, and the recorder's own can_we_sell() answers no and names the reasons. The page is the free scoreboard, and it is free forever: the whole record is on it. NO SAMPLE FILE, ON PURPOSE, AND sample_status IS 'fail' RATHER THAN 'on-page' FOR A REASON. There is no file behind this page to slice, so there is nothing to sample and the pill saying 'sample not ready' is correct. It is NOT 'on-page' either: on-page means the whole of what we hold is printed on the page, and that is false here -- the page prints every call, but the recorded grid load behind the threshold rule (hundreds of days of it) is counted on the page, not printed on it. Calling it on-page would be a sentence a stranger could check and find untrue. THERE IS NO UPLOAD SERVICE, no form, no account and no self-serve anything -- this estate's platform is not ours to add one to. The only way in is an email thread with a person, which is what the contact block on the page says. NO NUMBER, DATE, PRICE, GROUP, CADENCE OR BUYER IS TYPED INTO THE PAGE. scripts/slice_peak_call.py reads group, cadence, buyer and price out of this row with no fallback, and reads every call, date, hour, megawatt figure, fingerprint and count out of revenue-2026/var/peak_call.db read-only at build time. It recomputes every call's fingerprint with the recorder's own function on every build and refuses to write the page if one no longer matches, because the only claim this record makes is that it was not edited after the fact. It also reads the addresses the recorder fetches out of the recorder's own code and refuses to build unless each one carries a permission note whose verdict is 'allowed' -- a grid operator that refuses to be read is never named here as a source of anything. THE ZEROS ARE THE CONTENT, NOT A GAP. At 2026-08-25 no call had been scored yet and no call had told anyone to cut, and the page says both in words rather than printing an empty counter. The recorder's own written bar refuses a hit rate under 5 warnings, and refuses to call the record sellable under 60 scored calls, 5 warnings and 90 days of public record -- all three written down on 2026-08-24 while the answer to all three was still no. The page carries that bar and no percentage. cadence_long is NOT stored in this row on purpose: the module recounts it off the sealed calls at build time, so the page cannot go stale even if this row does. STILL TO WIRE, FOR WHOEVER MERGES THIS: there is no peak-call entry in scripts/family_status.py. That is harmless while this row lives in a fragment, because scripts/build_site.py reads catalog.json only and this family never reaches dist/. The day this row is merged into catalog.json it stops being harmless: the built page will carry no read-date stamp and scripts/check_built.py will mark it as a page with no read date. The store is at an absolute path, which _store_path() already supports.
